study.title: Cerebral Blood Flow Changes and Their Spatial Correlations With GABAa and Dopamine-D1 Receptor Explaining Individual Differences in Chronic Insomnia and the Therapeutic Effects of Acupuncture
study.study_design: Two-dataset study: (1) cross-sectional case-control neuroimaging study (Dataset 1); (2) randomized longitudinal neuroimaging study with acupuncture treatment or waitlist control (Dataset 2)
study.randomization: Participants in Dataset 2 were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the acupuncture treatment group or the waitlist control group using a computer-generated randomization sequence
study.blinding: Throughout the study, outcome assessors, data collectors, and statisticians remained blinded to the group assignments
study.population: Chronic insomnia disorder (CID) patients and healthy controls (HCs) recruited from outpatient clinics and surrounding communities
study.inclusion_criteria: Aligned with previous research (Shen et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2023); details in Supporting Information
study.exclusion_criteria: Aligned with previous research (Shen et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2023); details in Supporting Information

extraction_notes.note: No sham acupuncture arm was included in this study. The control for Dataset 2 was a waitlist group without any needle procedure. Sensory/interoceptive outcomes (e.g., deqi scales, pain ratings) were not quantitatively measured or reported as outcomes.
Expectancy, credibility, and blinding success (participant guessing allocation) were not assessed or reported in either dataset.
Adverse events were not reported in the main text. No statement was found explicitly saying that no adverse events occurred.

Detailed coordinate tables (Table S1, Table S3, Table S4) are referenced as supplementary materials but were not included in the provided PDF. Therefore, individual region coordinates and full cluster statistics for the 16 significant regions in Dataset 1 and the longitudinal results in Dataset 2 could not be extracted.

Table S1 (significant case-control CBF differences), Table S2 (within-group clinical outcomes acupuncture group), Table S3 (acupuncture group CBF changes), Table S4 (waitlist group CBF changes), and Table S5 (correlations between ΔCBF and clinical scores) are cited but not included in the PDF provided. Full statistical details and region-level results from these tables could not be extracted.

No MNI or Talairach coordinates were reported in the main text for any brain region. All region-level results are described by atlas parcellation labels (Schaefer 100 and HCP subcortical atlas) only. Coordinate fields are set to null accordingly.

The total N for neuroimaging analysis is reported as N=197 in the abstract (cross-sectional dataset), but after quality control the Dataset 1 total is 105 CID + 92 HC = 197. Dataset 2 total analyzed is 23 + 21 = 44. The n_total_analyzed_neuroimaging=197 refers to Dataset 1 only; Dataset 2 n=44 is separately reported.

The paper states '16 regions with statistically significant case-control differences' but only narratively describes some of them (visual cortex, dorsal attention network regions, left putamen, bilateral pallidum, bilateral diencephalon ventral). The complete list of all 16 regions is in Table S1 (supplement not provided).

The paper reports that within-group longitudinal CBF changes (Dataset 2) did not survive FDR correction, but significant results are reported at p<0.05 uncorrected. These uncorrected results are extracted as reported.

The paper states that the sample size calculation was based on 24 participants per group for Dataset 2 (48 total), but after exclusions 23 and 21 completed. The 48 total enrolled is used for n_total_randomized.

For Dataset 1, 108 CID + 96 HC = 204 enrolled; after QC exclusion (3 CID + 4 HC = 7 excluded), 197 analyzed. For Dataset 2, 48 randomized (24 per group); after exclusions (1 acupuncture + 3 waitlist = 4 excluded), 44 analyzed. The n_total_enrolled=245 is computed as 204+48=252 minus the 7 QC exclusions already applied differently, so the exact total enrolled figure is ambiguous. The value 245 is inferred as 108+96+24+24=252; however the paper does not state a single total enrolled figure. This is flagged as inferred.
The paper does not report global CBF values for Dataset 2 arms at either timepoint. Only Dataset 1 global CBF is reported (CID: 46.65 ± 6.39; HC: 46.77 ± 5.53).

The 3D T1-weighted structural image parameters (TR=7.06ms, TE=3.04ms, TI=450ms, FA=12°, FOV=256x256mm, matrix=256x256, 1mm thickness, no gap, 192 sagittal slices) are reported for both datasets as MRI acquisition parameters were consistent between datasets. ASL-specific post-label delay=2025ms, label duration=1450ms, 36 pairs of label and control volumes, FOV=240x240mm, reconstruction matrix=128x128, slice thickness=4mm, no gap, NEX=3, spiral readout 8 arms 512 sample points, FA=111°.

The CBF parcellation covered 100 cortical regions (Schaefer atlas) and 19 subcortical regions (HCP subcortical atlas), totaling 119 regions. Subcortical regions include bilateral cerebellum, thalamus, caudate, putamen, pallidum, hippocampus, amygdala, accumbens, diencephalon ventral, and brain stem.

Neurotransmitter receptor/transporter maps from the Neuromaps database (Hansen et al. 2022) include: dopamine (D1, D2, DAT), serotonin (5-HT1a, 5-HT1b, 5-HT2a, 5-HT4, 5-HT6, 5-HTT), acetylcholine (α4β2, M1, VAChT), GABA (GABAa), glutamate (NMDA, mGluR5), norepinephrine (NET), histamine (H3), cannabinoids (CB1), and opioids (MOR) — 15 receptors and 4 transporters.
The paper uses 'CBFglobal' notation for global CBF; in Dataset 1, CBFglobal was not significantly different between CID and HCs (CID: 46.65±6.39; HC: 46.77±5.53; t=0.04, p=0.97).
